newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Strong sales to flatten curve.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Strong sales to flatten curve.

text.p: Britain's gilt market faces a watershed this week in the shape of June retail sales figures which will go a long way to showing whether the consumer sector is chugging along steadily or is in the grip of an unsustainable boom.

Strong sales data will leave the market braced for a wave of interest rate rises and cause further inversion of an already-kinked curve. Subdued figures could allow shorter-dated gilts to recoup some lost ground.
But even that could be overshadowed by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony to Congress on Tuesday.
The September gilt future began the week on the back foot, dropping a quarter-point to 114-16 midway through Monday morning.
Don Smith, gilts analyst at HSBC Markets, said Greenspan could give bonds, gilts included, some support.

"We think that the testimony will provide the clearest indication yet of how far Greenspan has accepted the death of inflation thesis. Furthermore, we think there is a good chance that he will hint at a weaker GDP picture in Q2 than the markets expect."
But few will forget Greenspan's performance last November when he sent stocks and bonds spinning lower by warning of "irrational exuberance" in the markets.
"He could decide the bond market has got a bit ahead of itself and deliver a little warning. That could bring things to a crashing halt," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

Even if he does not, the good work may be undone by strong June retail sales figures. A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus forecasting a 0.4 percent rise in sales over the month, leaving them 4.5 percent up on a year ago.
That is healthy enough growth but Smith said latest surveys from the Confederation of British Industry and British Retail Consortium were consistent with a much stronger, one percent monthly rise.

"If we are right, then these data are set to reignite interest rate worries and apply upward pressure to yields at the short end of the curve," he said. As a result, the pressure for further curve inversion will increase.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said sales would not be nearly as strong as they were in May, when they leaped 1.1 percent, but the report was difficult to call.
"On the one hand, the bad weather will have disrupted sales. On the other, however, sales could have benefited from the filtering through of windfall gains," he said.
There is plenty else to occupy gilt investors this week aside from the Fed Governor and snapshot of British high streets.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown and Bank of England Governor Eddie George will testify to parliament's newly-appointed Treasury Select Committee on Tuesday and Wednesday respectively and GDP data are due on Friday.

Smith said the curve would invert further as signs of unbridled consumer spending force interest rate expectations higher and higher. Testimony from Brown and George will be sifted through for any clues on monetary policy as a result.

He said the long end of the market stood to benefit but would not move ahead until the auction of two billion pounds of 8.0 percent gilts due 2021 is out of the way. The Bank will hold the sale on Wednesday.

Scott said the 2021 stock had performed well in recent sessions and could be riding for a fall at Wednesday's auction. "If I was buying at the long end, I would be looking a little shorter than the 8.0s of 2021."
But like the other analysts, he agreed Greenspan would set the tone.

The week ends with the Confederation of British Industry releasing its distributive trades survey for July on Thursday, while the Office for National Statistics delivers preliminary GDP figures for the second quarter on Friday.
Economists forecast quarterly GDP growth of 0.9 percent and 3.4 percent year-on-year, well above the trend rate.

"We expect another robust GDP report in Q2, the service sector shows no sign of slowing," Barr said. "Indeed, we have been relatively conservative with our service sector quarterly forecast, implying that the risks to this forecast are on the upside."
He forecast 1.0 percent growth over the quarter.
